14-021.r: Cassini-Huygens → Saturn, not Venus; Messenger → mapped and orbited Mercury (2011–2015); Voyager 1 and 2 (launched 1977) → explore outer Solar System.

14-023.r: Cassini → NASA spacecraft to study Saturn; Apophis → asteroid; Spitzer → NASA infrared space telescope; TechSar → Israeli satellite launched by India's PSLV.

14-024.r: Evolved LISA (eLISA) → three spacecraft in an equilateral triangle, sides one million km, with lasers between them; detects gravitational waves; ESA-led with NASA.

14-026.r: Gravity Tractor (British, 2009) → a 10-ton spacecraft to stop asteroids from hitting Earth; idea proposed in 2005 by Edward T. Lu and Stanley G. Love.

14-027.r: Merger of giant black holes billions of light-years away → significance: gravitational waves were detected.

14-028.r: Gravitational waves first directly observed on 14 September 2015 by LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory); announced 11 February 2016.

14-029.r: Evidence cited for continued expansion of the universe → detection of microwaves in space and observation of redshift (answer: 1 and 2).

14-030.r: Expanding universe → based on Doppler effect; Edwin Hubble found light from distant galaxies shifted to the red end of the spectrum (red-shift).
14-030.c: The book says Christian Doppler came up with the idea in 1942; that is a misprint, he proposed it a century earlier.

14-031.r: Einstein's General Theory of Relativity predicts → light is affected by gravity, universe is expanding, matter warps surrounding space-time → all three.

14-032.r: Event Horizon, Singularity, String Theory, Standard Model → terms about observation and understanding of the Universe.

14-033.r: Black hole → a collapsed star; forms when very massive stars collapse at the end of their life cycle.

14-034.r: Black hole cannot be seen by telescope because its gravity is so strong that even light cannot escape → A and R true, R explains A.

14-035.r: Black hole → absorbs all radiations that fall on it, due to its high gravity.

14-036.r: Highly elongated elliptical orbit around the Sun → Comet; planets have nearly circular orbits.

14-037.r: Comet's tail → always points away from the Sun; solar radiation pushes dust (dust tail) and solar charged particles ionise gases (ion tail).

14-038.r: Photosphere ('light sphere') → bright outer layer of the Sun that emits most visible light; the other layers: chromosphere and corona.

14-040.r: Pulsars → rotating neutron stars emitting pulses of radiation at very regular intervals (milliseconds to seconds); have very strong magnetic fields.

14-041.r: Only one pair correct: Pulsars → neutron stars from collapsed massive stars. Cepheids → brighten and dim periodically; Nebulae → clouds of gas and dust (descriptions swapped).

14-042.r: Giant stars (eight to 100 times Sun's mass) → hotter, denser cores and faster nuclear reactions than dwarf stars, so they do not live longer → I wrong, II right.

14-043.r: Charged particles from space (several hundred km/sec) → diverted towards the poles by Earth's magnetic field; example: Aurora.

14-044.r: Major solar flare can → fail GPS/navigation, damage power grids, cause intense auroras, disturb satellite orbits, cut polar shortwave radio; not tsunamis or forest fires.

14-045.r: Re-entering space shuttle → air friction heats its surface and ionizes surrounding air, disturbing radio signals → brief loss of contact (A and R true, R explains A).

14-046.r: Geostationary satellite → about 36,000 km above the equator, not 10,000 km; FM music transmission is of very good quality as noise does little harm → only 2.
14-046.h: Three geostationary satellites, 120 degrees apart, cover the whole Earth; each sees about 40 percent.

14-047.r: Geostationary orbit → geosynchronous, circular, in Earth's equatorial plane; altitude about 35,786 km (22,236 miles), not 22,236 km; also called Clarke orbit.
14-047.t: Don't confuse 22,236 miles with km: the height is 35,786 km.

14-048.r: Geostatic position → object circles Earth at a speed matching Earth's, so it stays fixed (at fixed height) over a place on Earth; basis of geostationary satellites.

14-050.r: Communication satellites → located in the exosphere, the outermost and extremely thin layer of the atmosphere.

14-051.r: Geostationary satellite → period of revolution 24 hours, same as Earth's rotation period.

14-053.r: Path of a geostationary satellite in space → circular (option a diagram).

14-054.r: Kepler space telescope (NASA, 2009) → to find Earth-like planets around other stars; retired 30 October 2018 after 9 years; found more than 2600 exoplanets.

14-055.r: Chandra X-ray telescope → named after Indian-American astrophysicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar; launched by Space Shuttle Columbia on 23 July 1999.
14-055.t: Not C.V. Raman, J.C. Bose or P.C. Roy, though all have 'Chandra' in their names.

14-056.r: Astrosat → India's first dedicated multiwavelength space observatory, PSLV-XL, 28 September 2015; statements 'only USA, Russia before' and '2000 kg at 1650 km' both wrong.

14-057.r: IceCube → world's biggest neutrino telescope, completed December 2010, designed by the University of Wisconsin.

14-058.r: Highest ground-based telescope observatory now → University of Tokyo Atacama Observatory, Chile (5,640 m); at question time → Indian Astronomical Observatory, Hanle, Ladakh. The book gives no single answer (*).

14-059.r: MACE (Hanle, Ladakh) → Asia's largest, world's highest imaging Cherenkov telescope, about 4,270 m (not 5100); inaugurated 4 October 2024 by Ajit Kumar Mohanty; built by BARC.

14-060.r: ISRO = Indian Space Research Organisation → India's space agency under the Department of Space; earlier INCOSPAR, set up in 1962.

14-061.r: INSAT-3B launch (21 March 2000, Ariane 5G, Kourou, French Guiana) → ISRO Chairman was K. Kasturirangan (headed ISRO 1994–2003).

14-062.r: ISRO Chairman when asked → G. Madhavan Nair; present Chairman → Dr. V. Narayanan (since 13 January 2025). The book gives no single answer (*).

14-063.r: ISRO chairmen: A.S. Kiran Kumar 2015–2018; 10th → S. Somanath 2022–2025; 11th, present → V. Narayanan (from 13 January 2025); first → Vikram Sarabhai.

14-065.r: Current ISRO Chairman → Dr. V. Narayanan (from 13 January 2025), succeeding Dr. S. Somanath (January 2022 to January 2025). The book gives no single answer (*).

14-066.r: INSAT → ISRO's multipurpose geostationary satellites for telecommunication, broadcasting, meteorology; India's telecom is satellite-linked, but not for 'star war' (A true, R false).
